picked.t: Vietnam needs $300B in annual investment, productivity gains to achieve double-digit growth
picked.body: Such rapid growth is not unprecedented in Asia: Singapore's economy expanded by 12.1% a year from 1967-1973 while South Korea's grew at 10.8% in 1986-1988. For Vietnam, achieving the growth is key to its goal of reaching high-income status by 2045. Achieving the growth target hinges on its ability to mobilize resources, allocate and use such resources efficiently, and boost productivity, according to experts at the 2026 Autumn Economic Forum held last week. Dr. Can Van Luc, a member of the National Financial and Monetary Policy Advisory Council, said an investment-to-GDP ratio of 35-40% was a common trait seen in economies like Singapore, South Korea, and China during their periods of rapid growth. Vietnam needs to keep total investment in the economy at around 40% of GDP, he said. "Given the growth target and this investment ratio, we (the council) estimate that Vietnam needs to mobilize $280-300 billion annually, with the amount increasing by around 14% each year." Public investment, which accounts for 20-22% of the total, could cover up to 30% of the amount needed and so the remaining 70% must come from other sources, including the private sector and foreign investment, he said. He also stressed the need to develop the capital market as the stock and corporate bond markets currently account for just 13-14% of investment, while banks make up 51%. Wanming Du, director of index policy for Asia-Pacific at FTSE Russell, forecast that banks would continue to play an important role, but as the economy grows, financing needs would become increasingly diverse and complex. "That is why a deep and well-functioning capital market is absolutely vital. It also helps strengthen the diversity and resilience of the entire financial system." But investing efficiently is just as important as securing more capital. Major Asian economies posted incremental capital-output ratios (ICORs) of three to four during their periods of rapid growth, with a lower ratio reflecting more efficient use of capital. Vietnam recorded ICORs of above six in the last five years. Luc said Vietnam should aim to lower the ratio to 4.5 by shifting public investment into science and technology, education, and healthcare from the current 80% it allocates to infrastructure. Boosting productivity Vietnam needs to improve productivity at every level, from the public sector and state-owned enterprises to private businesses and foreign-invested companies, according to experts. Mariam J. Sherman, World Bank's division director for Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, said a Vietnamese manufacturing worker currently generates around $6.7 in value added per hour, less than half the level in China. Meanwhile, around 85% of jobs in the export sector involve manufacturing activities such as assembly. Growth in Vietnam's total factor productivity (TFP), which gauges how efficiently an economy turns its inputs into outputs, has virtually stalled since 1990, she said. Denis Depoux, global managing director of Germany-based consultancy Roland Berger, said manufacturing accounts for 36% of Vietnam's GDP. The share reaches almost 80% when manufacturing-related services are included, he said. So the key to TFP growth will involve innovation and modernizing the industrial value chain, he noted. Experts at the AEF 2026 noted that Vietnam has ample opportunities to help it achieve double-digit growth, but executing policies effectively while ensuring that macroeconomic stability is not compromised in pursuit of growth is a challenge. World Bank's Sherman said Vietnam is "at the threshold of its second great transformation," one that "should move firms up the value chain, workers into better jobs, and the State from directing the economy to enabling it."

picked.t: AppotaPay showcases payment solutions for retailers, restaurant chains at VIFS 2026
picked.body: AppotaPay showcased its payment solutions at the Vietnam International Franchise Show (VIFS) 2026, held from Oct. 29 to 31 at the Saigon Exhibition and Convention Center in Ho Chi Minh City. The event brought together domestic and international brands, franchisors, restaurant operators and retail technology providers. AppotaPay also introduced two reports examining purchasing power and consumer spending in Vietnam's retail and food and beverage (F&B) sectors, drawing on official statistics and third-party research to identify trends relevant to business planning for 2027. The retail report said sales of retail goods in Vietnam rose 12.8% year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026. An InsightAsia survey of 1,236 consumers aged 18-45 in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City found that 49% considered fast checkout and payment "very important" when choosing a convenience store. The F&B report highlighted a gap between consumer spending intentions and business expansion plans. About 35% of surveyed consumers expected to reduce F&B spending in the second half of 2026, while 52% of surveyed businesses planned to expand. The findings highlighted the importance of monitoring consumer demand and operating costs when planning business expansion. Payment solutions for physical and online businesses At the exhibition, AppotaPay demonstrated services designed to manage transactions across physical stores and online channels. Its SmartPOS terminals accept domestic and international bank cards, e-wallets and QR code payments through a single device. Businesses can use them at checkout counters or restaurant tables, track transactions by store or shift, and manage employee access. The AppotaPay Partner platform provides centralized revenue and transaction monitoring across multiple outlets, along with automated payment reconciliation. For online businesses, the company offers a payment gateway for websites and mobile applications, as well as Payment Link, which allows merchants to collect payments for orders placed through social media and messaging platforms. Other features include automatic payment notifications and virtual accounts that help identify and reconcile incoming bank transfers. AppotaPay also introduced QR Global , a cross-border payment service for businesses serving international visitors. The service supports QR payments through selected banking applications and e-wallets from China, South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. Customers can scan merchants' QR codes using supported applications from their home markets, while merchants receive settlements in Vietnamese dong after automatic currency conversion. Integrated into AppotaPay's SmartPOS and SoftPOS solutions, QR Global provides an additional payment option for retailers, restaurants and hospitality businesses serving international customers. A member of Appota Group, AppotaPay provides payment acceptance, collection, disbursement and transaction management services. The company says it serves more than 600 business customers and supports around 30,000 transaction points nationwide. It is licensed by the State Bank of Vietnam to provide payment intermediary services. In March 2026, AppotaPay received PCI DSS Level 1 certification for the fourth consecutive year, meeting international payment card data security requirements.

picked.t: Ho Chi Minh City well positioned to become connected growth hub: WEF CEO
picked.body: Stephan Mergenthaler, CEO of the World Economic Forum (WEF), said HCMC was well positioned to strengthen its role as a connected growth hub, linking Vietnamese businesses with global investors and technology partners. Speaking at the opening plenary session of the 2026 Autumn Economic Forum in HCMC on Oct. 28, Mergenthaler identified three major drivers of global economic growth whose convergence could benefit Vietnam and its largest economic hub. The first is intelligence, which can boost productivity, strengthen competitiveness, create better jobs, and raise living standards. The second is the need to develop sustainable and resilient industries. "For a dynamic manufacturing economy like Vietnam, this development is particularly important," Mergenthaler said. The third is connectivity, which brings together ideas, capital, talent, and markets. Cities play a key role by fostering innovation ecosystems where businesses and entrepreneurs can turn global opportunities into local economic activity, he said. "We can see this right here in HCMC, which has many favorable conditions to strengthen its position as one of the highly connected growth hubs." He cited the city's vibrant startup ecosystem, industrial capabilities, and commitment to international cooperation as foundations for linking Vietnamese enterprises with global investors and technology partners. HCMC is home to more than 40 incubators and innovation centers and has a dynamic, open economy. In the first nine months of 2026, the city's gross regional domestic product (GRDP) grew 9.06% year-on-year. Exports reached approximately US$76 billion, up 10.6%, while foreign direct investment (FDI) exceeded $17.8 billion, an increase of 323.1%. HCMC People's Committee Chairman Nguyen Van Duoc said the city's expanded administrative boundaries following its merger with neighboring localities had created new development opportunities and strengthened links among urban areas, industry, science, technology, and innovation. Echoing Mergenthaler's emphasis on connectivity, Duoc said stronger integration was essential to the city's next stage of development. The city's financial center, innovation ecosystem, and logistics sector could not operate in isolation but needed to become part of broader financial, trade, and supply chain networks. Such connections would bring together capital, technology, knowledge, talent, and markets, creating new economic opportunities, he said. "For HCMC, developing through stronger connections with other localities, industries, urban centers, financial and technology hubs, innovation ecosystems, and international partners is an objective necessity and an imperative," Duoc said. The 2026 Autumn Economic Forum took place from Oct. 26 to 29, bringing together global science, technology, and innovation organizations, hundreds of international businesses, industry associations, and diplomatic representatives. It was the second time HCMC had hosted the forum and its first partnership and co-branding arrangement with the WEF.

picked.t: 빈그룹 총수, 빈패스트에 4.4억 달러 추가 투자…우선주 매입
picked.body: 팜 녓 브엉 빈그룹 창업자 겸 회장. (사진=빈그룹) 베트남 최대 민간기업 빈그룹(Vingroup)을 이끄는 팜 녓 브엉(Pham Nhat Vuong) 회장이 4억3,600만 달러 규모 우선주 매입으로 빈패스트(VinFast)에 대한 추가 투자에 나선 것으로 나타났다. 빈패스트가 최근 미국 증권거래위원회(SEC)에 제출한 자료에 따르면, 브엉 회장은 우선주 매입을 통해 빈패스트베트남에 4억3,600만 달러를 추가 투자했다. 빈패스트베트남이 브엉 회장에게 발행한 주식은 전환권 없는 배당 우선주다. 우선주는 일반 주주보다 배당을 먼저, 더 많이 받을 수 있으나, 의결권이 제한되는 것이 일반적이다. 이에 대해 빈패스트는 “브엉 회장의 이번 투자는 당사의 성장을 뒷받침하기 위한 것”이라고 설명했다. 앞서 베트남 증권사 중 하나인 비엣캡증권(Vietcap)은 지난달 21일 빈패스트가 주최한 투자자 간담회 이후 분석을 통해 빈패스트베트남이 해당 자금을 통해 ‘올림픽응옥호이(Olympic Ngoc Hoi)’ 프로젝트의 합작 투자사인 응옥호이부동산을 인수할 가능성이 있다고 전망한 바 있다. 해당 프로젝트는 총 9,171헥타르에 걸쳐 925조7,000억 동(358억7,490만여 달러)이 투자될 예정이다. 빈패스트의 초소형 전기차 VF3. 비엣캡증권에 따르면, 브엉 회장은 2분기 말 기준 빈패스트베트남의 모기업인 빈패스트에 약 40조5,000억 동(약 15억6,960만 달러)을 추가로 투자했다. 앞서 브엉 회장은 “가진 돈이 모두 바닥날 때까지 빈패스트에 대한 투자를 지속할 것”이라고 밝히기도 했다. 브엉 회장은 370억 달러가 넘는 순자산으로 동남아 최대 부호에 올라있다. 그는 빈그룹과 개인 회사를 통해 빈패스트의 지배지분을 확보하고 있다. 자본금 35조 동의 빈패스트베트남은 지난 6월 모기업의 계열 분리를 통해 제조 부문을 제3자에게 위탁하며 설립됐다. 계열 분리 이후, 빈패스트베트남은 빈패스트커머셜&서비스트레이딩(VinFast Commercial & Services Trading LLC), 빈패스트엔지니어링오스트레일리아(VinFast Engineering Australia Pty Ltd), 빈패스트독일(VinFast Germany GmbH) 등의 모든 지분을 보유하며, △전 세계 제품 연구개발(R&D) △A/S △판매 사업을 담당한다.

picked.t: Company of Southeast Asia’s richest man posts first $1B quarterly profit
picked.body: Vietnam’s largest listed company saw revenue almost quadruple year-on-year to VND150.58 trillion, according to the company’s financial report. As in the first two quarters, real estate generated the largest share of revenue, at nearly VND98.5 trillion, or more than 65% of the total. By September-end, Vingroup held nearly VND107 trillion in cash and bank deposits. During the period, it also raised about $2.3 billion through bond issuance, the sale of preferred shares and syndicated loans from international investors. Since 2025, Vingroup has expanded into power and infrastructure, alongside traditional businesses including real estate, industrial manufacturing and technology. Real estate, however, remains the main growth driver for the conglomerate led by billionaire Vuong. VNDirect Securities estimates that real estate will remain Vingroup’s mainstay, contributing at least 50% of its total revenue and profit over the next five years. Meanwhile, its electric vehicle, infrastructure and energy businesses are expected to expand rapidly, raising their combined share of the group’s revenue to 30%–40% over the long term. This year, Vuong’s conglomerate is developing a series of major projects across the country. In real estate, it is building several urban areas spanning thousands of hectares, including projects in Quang Ninh, Hanoi and HCMC. In infrastructure, Vingroup, through its subsidiaries, is involved in engineering, procurement and construction contracts for five urban railway lines in Hanoi, with a total value of about $49 billion. Vuong, chairman of Vingroup, is the richest man in Southeast Asia with $37.7 billion in net worth, according to real-time data by Forbes.

picked.t: Vietnam must be more strategically proactive amid global uncertainty: PM
picked.body: Vietnam must take a more proactive strategic approach, strengthen domestic capabilities, and expand international cooperation as global economic and geopolitical uncertainties intensify, PM Hung said. Speaking at a dialogue with World Economic Forum (WEF) CEO Stephan Mergenthaler during the 2026 Autumn Economic Forum in HCMC on Oct. 28, Hung outlined Vietnam's response to global economic shifts and its development ambitions for the next decade. The 60-minute dialogue was a highlight of the forum. Mergenthaler opened by asking how Vietnam viewed global changes and their implications for the country's development. The Vietnamese leader said the world was undergoing profound changes, with shifts in the balance of power accelerating the emergence of a more multipolar international order. Strategic competition among major powers is intensifying and extending into economics, technology, data, energy, and standards governing trade, investment, the environment, and governance. Globalization is continuing but becoming more fragmented, with greater emphasis on security, self-reliance, and resilience. Meanwhile, rapid advances in science, technology, and artificial intelligence are transforming production, governance, and the distribution of economic advantages and development resources. These changes pose major challenges, including the need to update international institutions and rules, declining strategic trust amid intensifying competition, and the diminishing effectiveness of traditional growth models, particularly in developing economies. Vietnam therefore needs to strengthen its resilience, strategic autonomy, and capacity to generate new sources of growth, Hung said. "The more uncertain the world becomes, the more strategically proactive Vietnam must be, strengthening its internal capabilities and expanding cooperation," he said. "Vietnam will continue to be a friend, a reliable partner, and a responsible member of the international community, as well as a stable and safe destination for partners and investors." Five priorities to strengthen economic resilience Asked how Vietnam would improve its resilience, Hung outlined five priorities. The first is maintaining political and social stability while strengthening macroeconomic fundamentals, which he described as essential to sustaining confidence among citizens and domestic and foreign businesses. Vietnam will continue to manage macroeconomic policies flexibly to maintain stability, major economic balances, energy security, and food security. Public debt currently stands at around 34% of GDP, giving the country fiscal room to support households and businesses during economic shocks while continuing to invest in strategic infrastructure and development priorities, he said. The second priority is institutional reform, including aligning the legal framework with international standards and practices and removing barriers to business and investment. Third, Vietnam will accelerate infrastructure development, particularly in transport, ports, energy, and other essential facilities. It will also strengthen technological capabilities and links between domestic companies and foreign-invested enterprises. "Vietnam will attract investment selectively, with an emphasis on technology transfer and workforce training and development," Hung said. The remaining priorities are improving the quality and effectiveness of education and training, and strengthening foreign relations while diversifying partnerships to create more development opportunities. Maintaining strategic autonomy Mergenthaler also asked how Vietnam could maintain strategic autonomy amid declining international trust and intensifying competition among major powers. Hung said strategic autonomy meant building domestic capabilities to preserve the country's ability to make independent decisions and choose partnerships that serve national interests while respecting other countries' legitimate interests. Vietnam will focus on improving economic competitiveness, supporting domestic businesses, and advancing science, technology, and innovation. It will also safeguard national sovereignty and security, including energy, food, environmental, and human security, while diversifying essential supply chains to reduce exposure to external shocks. At the same time, Vietnam will pursue international integration and make effective use of its 18 signed free trade agreements to expand markets, diversify partners, and attract capital, technology, and knowledge. "Our goal is not only to participate more deeply in global value chains but also to strengthen domestic capabilities, gradually master technologies, and generate greater added value for the Vietnamese economy," Hung said. Vietnam's role in the global economy Asked about Vietnam's ambitions in the evolving global economic landscape through 2035, Hung said the country aims to become an emerging hub for digital technology, new and green energy, and green agriculture. picked.t: Vietnam lowers electricity price, first time in almost 20 years
picked.body: Average retail price is now at VND2,159.90 per kilowatt-hour, according to the Vietnam Electricity. This is the first decrease in the average electricity price in nearly 20 years, excluding five rounds of reductions in electricity bills and prices to support people and businesses affected by Covid-19. Between 2023 and 2025, electricity prices rose by 18.2% in four adjustments. The last increase was made in May 2025. Before those increases, electricity prices had remained unchanged for more than four years, from March 2019 to May 2023. EVN said the reduction followed a review of its operations and efforts to calculate and cut costs as much as possible. The adjustment is intended to support people and businesses, help stabilize the macroeconomy and ensure social welfare. At a National Assembly session on economic and social issues on the morning of Oct. 31, Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang said the government had directed EVN to cut costs as much as possible to lower average retail electricity prices by about 2%. He said the electricity price reduction, together with a plan to cut the special consumption tax on gasoline to zero, would provide about 0.07 percentage points of additional room to control inflation and work toward the 4.5% target set by the National Assembly.
